hints: Look closely at the structure of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and ask whether it is primary, secondary or tertiary.
Recall that a tertiary halogenoalkane favours SN1, so the C-Cl bond breaks first to give a stable carbocation intermediate.
Now join that carbocation to the actual nucleophile given, $\text{CH}_3\text{O}^-$, and see which product is an ether containing O-CH3.
walkthrough:
**Identify the halogenoalkane type**

2-chloro-2-methylpropane is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}$. The carbon bonded to Cl is bonded to three other carbons, so it is tertiary.

$$ (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-Cl} \text{ : tertiary halogenoalkane} $$

**Choose SN1 or SN2**

Tertiary halogenoalkanes are too hindered for SN2 backside attack. They react by SN1, with slow loss of $\text{Cl}^-$ to form a stable tertiary carbocation.

$$ (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-Cl} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+ + \text{Cl}^- $$

**Attack by the nucleophile to give the product**

The nucleophile here is methoxide, $\text{CH}_3\text{O}^-$, not hydroxide. It attacks the carbocation to form an ether.

$$ (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+ + \text{CH}_3\text{O}^- \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COCH}_3 $$

**Match to the table**

We need a carbocation intermediate $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ and the ether product $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COCH}_3$. That matches only one row.

options.A: Correct. SN1 intermediate is the tertiary carbocation $(CH_3)_3C^+$ and attack by $CH_3O^-$ gives the methyl ether $(CH_3)_3COCH_3$.
options.B: The intermediate is right for SN1, but the product is wrong. $(CH_3)_3CCH_2OH$ adds an extra carbon and contains an alcohol OH group. The nucleophile is $CH_3O^-$, so oxygen must stay attached to CH3 to give an ether.
options.C: This shows an SN2 transition state $[Nu---C---Cl]^-$, which is wrong for a tertiary substrate. It also uses the wrong nucleophile fragment $HOCH_2-$, giving an alcohol product instead of the methoxy ether.
options.D: The product $H_3COC(CH_3)_3$ is correct, but the mechanism is wrong. $[H_3CO---C(CH_3)_3---Cl]^-$ is an SN2 transition state. A tertiary chloride is too hindered for SN2 and reacts via the SN1 carbocation instead.
